acceptable.choice: A hosted booking and class-scheduling service with built-in card payments, embedded in the Webflow site, such as Bookwhen, SimplyBook.me, Acuity Scheduling or Square Appointments/Classes
acceptable.why: It covers capacity limits, deposits, confirmations, reminders, cancellations and secure card checkout without any back end, at about 30×8 bookings a month, for a monthly fee the client can pay and own.

acceptable.choice: Square (bookings plus payments), if the studio already uses or wants a Square till for in-person sales
acceptable.why: One account covers studio sales, workshop bookings and deposits, so there's less to hand over and the client already knows the tool.

acceptable.choice: Calendly group event types with Stripe or PayPal payment, charging the deposit amount
acceptable.why: It's cheap, familiar and easy to embed, and it caps places per session; a good fit if the studio's needs are simple.

acceptable.choice: Ticketing platforms such as Eventbrite or Tito, with a 'deposit' ticket price
acceptable.why: They take no setup work and enforce capacity; acceptable if the client accepts per-ticket fees and the platform's branding.

acceptable.choice: Stripe Payment Links (one per workshop, with a payment limit of 8) linked from Webflow CMS pages
acceptable.why: It's the cheapest no-code option with no subscription and no server, but it's only a fallback: it needs manual setup every month and has no rescheduling, waitlist or customer emails.

ruled_out.choice: A custom back end (Node/Express, Django, Laravel, Rails) on a VPS or PaaS with its own database
ruled_out.why: The designer has never written a back end, so they couldn't hand it over or maintain it safely. It brings security, payment-webhook and uptime duties, and it costs more than the problem justifies.

ruled_out.choice: Custom serverless functions plus Stripe Checkout plus Supabase/Firebase/Airtable, built by the coding agent
ruled_out.why: It looks cheap, but it is still a payment system the designer must debug, secure and support. Overbooking races, refunds and webhook failures would land on someone who can't diagnose them, and other freelancers couldn't take it over.

ruled_out.choice: Building a reusable multi-tenant booking SaaS of their own to resell to clients
ruled_out.why: It turns a freelancer into a software vendor with ongoing payment-security responsibility. The reuse goal is better met by a repeatable setup of an existing tool.

ruled_out.choice: Moving the site to WordPress with WooCommerce Bookings or similar plugins
ruled_out.why: It throws away the Webflow site and the designer's workflow, and adds hosting, plugin updates and security patching that the client can't handle.

ruled_out.choice: Webflow Ecommerce with each workshop as a product limited to 8 in stock
ruled_out.why: It isn't a booking system: there are no session dates, reminders, cancellations, rescheduling or proper deposit handling, it needs manual product setup each month, and it requires a more expensive plan with transaction fees.

ruled_out.choice: Zapier/Make glue between forms, a spreadsheet and Stripe
ruled_out.why: It breaks easily, can overbook under concurrent bookings, stacks several subscriptions, and is hard for the client or another freelancer to understand when something breaks.

ruled_out.choice: Any setup where card details pass through or are stored on the site or the designer's code
ruled_out.why: It breaks PCI rules and creates liability for both the designer and the client.
The cost and complexity are far beyond what a single small ceramics studio needs.

must_mention: They very likely don't need a custom back end at all. A hosted booking tool with integrated payments, embedded or linked from Webflow, is the right default at this size (about 240 places a month).
Card payments should go through a hosted checkout (Stripe, Square, PayPal) so card data never touches the site, which keeps PCI compliance out of the designer's hands.
The client should own the payment account (Stripe/Square) and the booking-tool subscription in their own name, with the designer added as a collaborator. That's what makes handover clean.
Check that the chosen tool supports group or class sessions with a capacity limit (8 places) and deposits or part-payment, and decide how the balance is collected (online later or in the studio).
Costs: a monthly subscription (roughly free to tens of dollars) plus card processing fees (around 1.5–3% plus a fixed amount per transaction). Compare these against the client's budget.
Reuse comes from picking one tool and documenting a standard setup and embed process to repeat for each client, not from writing shared code.
Cancellation and refund policy, confirmation and reminder emails, and how the studio adds the roughly 30 workshops each month should be settled as part of the setup.
red_flags: Recommending that they write and host their own booking or payment back end, even 'with the coding agent's help', without clearly saying this is unnecessary and risky for them.
Any design that collects or stores raw card numbers, or builds card forms outside a provider's hosted or embedded elements.
Setting up the Stripe or booking account under the designer's own name, or routing client money through the designer.
Ignoring capacity and overbooking, for example a plain form plus a payment link with no seat limit.
Suggesting the client leave Webflow or rebuild the site just to get bookings.
Implying payments are free, or leaving out processing and subscription fees.
Presenting specific features (deposits, group classes, regional availability, prices) as definite without telling the designer to check the vendor's current plans.
Over-engineering for 'reuse', such as building a multi-client platform, instead of a repeatable no-code setup.
unknowns: The client's country and currency, which affect which booking tools and payment providers are available and whether strong customer authentication (SCA) applies.
Exactly how the deposit works: a fixed or percentage amount, whether the balance is charged online later or paid in the studio, and the refund or cancellation terms.
The client's budget for a monthly subscription versus per-booking fees.
Whether the studio already uses a till or payment system (such as Square or SumUp) that would make one tool the obvious choice.
Whether they need extras: waitlists, gift vouchers, multi-week courses, private group bookings, discount codes, or calendar sync for staff.
The current Webflow site plan, and whether it allows custom-code embeds, or whether an external booking page link is acceptable.
Who will add workshops and handle changes day to day (the studio or the designer), which affects how simple the admin side must be.
How similar the other clients' needs are, which determines whether one standard tool can really be reused for all of them.
